chunks: From him, from Hisham ibn Salim and others, from 'Ammar al-Sabati, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who gave permission to his slave to marry a woman, and he married her; then the slave ran away (abandoned his master). He said: 'She has no maintenance (nafaqah) from her master, and her bond of marriage has been severed from him, for the running away of the slave is the divorce of his wife, and he is like the one who apostatizes from Islam.'

I said: 'If he returns to his masters, will his wife return to him?' He said: 'If her waiting period (iddah) had expired from him, and then she married another man, there is no way for him to reclaim her; but if she did not marry and the waiting period had not expired, she is his wife upon the first marriage.'

key_terms.إِبَاق: Running away or desertion of a slave from his master
key_terms.عِدَّتُهَا: The waiting period for a woman after separation or death
key_terms.عِصْمَتُهَا: The bond or sanctity of marriage
key_terms.نَفَقَةٌ: Maintenance or financial support provided to the wife

ai.seo_question: What is the legal status of a slave's marriage if he runs away from his master?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) elucidates that a slave's flight (abq) acts as an irrevocable divorce, severing the master's obligation for maintenance and the marital bond, akin to the status of an apostate. This ruling highlights the unique legal agency of the slave in this context, where the master's initial permission does not prevent the dissolution upon departure. The hadith further clarifies the conditions for reinstatement, emphasizing that remarriage during the waiting period (iddah) finalizes the divorce, a principle rooted in the Quranic verses on divorce and waiting periods.
